cells.tense: Right now, something is arriving and your hands are already open to it.
cells.act: meet what is arriving as it arrives
cells.ask: For an ordinary thing you'd normally pick up mid-thought, meet it as it arrives — pause, let it be new, then take it up. Do that a few times across two or three days.
cells.core:
Something is finishing, and you can feel the finisher in it. The last stretch of a project, a change of season, a way of living that ran its course — the close is inside you, and what is arriving is coming in freely. Your hands are open, not clenched, so the end doesn't feel like a loss and the start doesn't feel like a threat. You recognize the turning as yours. That's why the next thing can enter without you having to explain it first.

What's already working keeps working when the door isn't forced. This doesn't stay done by itself — the odds are you keep finding something already closed and reopening it just to check. This week, take something you'd normally call unfinished, and stop carrying it past its end. Let it be finished without announcing it. The next thing has your hands.
cells.sheetLine: Something is closing. Your hands are still open for what comes next.
cells.verb: Finishing the thing — integration that releases into what's opening next
cells.place: The threshold where something outside is arriving and about to be let in

cells.tense: You've already arrived at a finish line nobody can see from where they stand.
cells.act: receive the thing that is coming instead of bracing for it
cells.ask: Look at what you actually did in the last stretch of the thing you're calling done — the real moves, not the story. Let that reach you before you decide anything. Then, if it's still open, leave it open a week.
cells.core:
You're living at the far end of the story, saying the thing is done while the middle is still being written. The declaration goes first, and you build backward from it — the announcement of a launch, a chapter closed, a self you've already arrived at. It's a real skill at speed. Here it's running past where you actually are, so the work you still have to do gets less time than the banner you've already hung.

The arrival belongs to other people's eyes; your part is the sentence coming next. Let what actually happened reach you instead of bracing for the version you already announced. If a piece is still open, it stays open — you can still be a person who finishes things, and just be telling the truth about which.

cells.tense: You packed a life around a door you didn't walk through long before now.
cells.act: take the turning as it comes
cells.ask: Put in a single sentence something you're still carrying as unfinished — a hope, a project, a version of yourself — ending on what it was. Then leave the page alone for a day.
cells.core:
You still wear the coat of a project you started long back, take its temperature weekly, call it not-done. The trunk didn't get put down, but nothing is being built on it either. Mornings go to keeping an old door open rather than to what is actually arriving now, and the doors near you mostly go unanswered. From inside it looks like patience. You still think the work is on hold.

Nothing needs to be resolved. Write a single sentence about something you're still holding as in progress, ending on what it was. Leave it alone for a day. You do not have to arrive anywhere. What is already past simply gets to be past, and your hands come back for what's here.

cells.tense: You set something down without noticing your fingers still on it.
cells.act: let go of the thing you are gripping
cells.ask: Across four evenings, notice what you are still gripping and whether it is done. Where it is done, set it down on purpose: a line on paper, then close the book for the night.
cells.core:
The endings in your life were real, but you didn't write them — the job changed, the season turned, the people moved on, and something in you didn't sign off. Now some of what's past is still carried as a debt, and some of what's finished is kept open as a matter of course. You walk through completed rooms believing you might have to answer for them.

What needs doing is not a reckoning but a look. Each evening, notice what you're still gripping and whether it's actually full and gone. If it is, lay it down. Not a cleanout — one object a night, at your own pace. Knowing which door is behind you is yours to do. What you've already finished stops needing a hand to balance it.
